English

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Contraction of fundamental, originating in Indian English.

Noun

[edit]

funda (countable and uncountable, plural fundas or fundae or fundaes)

  1. (India) Basics or fundamentals, considered as a unit.
    Get your funda correct before you submit the paper.
    What is the funda behind relativity?
    • 1992 [1]
      In my opinion, the funda is as follows:
  2. (India) Understanding.
    • 1993, [2]
      You did not have the funda to realize that the statistics is an ass.
    • 1993, [3]
      But then, your funda is weak.

Usage notes

[edit]

Whilst fundaes and fundae both occur as the plural of funda, fundas is far more widespread. The pluralization to fundae is by analogy to formula/formulae. The pluralization to fundas is by the simple addition of -s.

The word is frequently used in Indian quizzing circles to denote the interesting fact or concept behind a question.

See also

[edit]
  • fundu

References

[edit]
  • Usenet posting by Sivakumar Ravada, prescribing fundae as the plural
  • IITM lingo, accessed on 2005-05-09, prescribing fundaes as the plural
  • The Fundoo Funda, some comments about the words funda and fundoo.

Galician

[edit]

Etymology 1

[edit]

Attested with this meaning since the 14th century. Learned borrowing from Late Latin funda (“bag”), from Latin funda. Doublet of fonda. Compare Portuguese fonda and Spanish funda and honda.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): [ˈfundɐ]

Noun

[edit]

funda f (plural fundas)

  1. case, cover
    Synonym: estoxo
    • c. 1350, Lourdes Soriano, editor, Livro de Tristan:
      Quando eles uirõ Lãça[rote] nõ no conoçerõ porque fezera el meter seu escudo em sua fonda
      When they saw Lancelot they didn't recognise him, because he ordered to put his shield inside its case
  2. overalls
    Synonym: mono

References

[edit]
  • Seoane, Ernesto Xosé González; Granja, María Álvarez de la; Agrelo, Ana Isabel Boullón (2006–2022), “funda”, in Dicionario de Dicionarios do galego medieval [Dictionary of dictionaries of Medieval Galician] (in Galician), Santiago de Compostela: Instituto da Lingua Galega
  • Barreiro, Xavier Varela; Guinovart, Xavier Gómez (2006–2018), “funda”, in Corpus Xelmírez: corpus lingüístico da Galicia medieval [Corpus Xelmírez: linguistic corpus of Medieval Galicia] (in Galician), Santiago de Compostela: Instituto da Lingua Galega
  • Antón Luís Santamarina Fernández, editor (2006–2013), “funda”, in Dicionario de Dicionarios da lingua galega [Dictionary of Dictionaries of the Galician language] (in Galician), Santiago de Compostela: Instituto da Lingua Galega
  • Antón Luís Santamarina Fernández, Ernesto Xosé González Seoane, María Álvarez de la Granja, editors (2003–2018), “funda”, in Tesouro informatizado da lingua galega (in Galician), Santiago de Compostela: Instituto da Lingua Galega
  • Rosario Álvarez Blanco, editor (2014–2024), “funda”, in Tesouro do léxico patrimonial galego e portugués (in Galician), Santiago de Compostela: Instituto da Lingua Galega, →ISSN

Etymology 2

[edit]

funda

    1. first/third-person singular present subjunctive

Latin

[edit]
Latin Wikipedia has an article on:
funda
Wikipedia la

Etymology 1

[edit]

Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰondʰeh₂, from *bʰendʰ- (“to bind”), whence English bind. Alternatively, a loanword from an unknown language, which may also have been the source of Ancient Greek σφενδόνη (sphendónē, “sling”).[1]

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (Classical Latin) IPA(key): [ˈfʊn.da]
  • (modern Italianate Ecclesiastical) IPA(key): [ˈfun.da]

Noun

[edit]

funda f (genitive fundae); first declension

  1. a hand-sling
    Coordinate term: fustibalus (“a sling-staff, a stick sling”)
Declension
[edit]

First-declension noun.

singular plural

dative fundae fundīs

vocative funda fundae

  • *fundula (diminutive) (Vulgar Latin)
    • ⇒ Vulgar Latin: *fundla (contraction)
      • ⇒ Vulgar Latin: *flunda (metathesis)
        • Asturian: flonda, fronda
        • French: fronde
          • → Italian: fronda
        • Italian: fionda
        • Sicilian: ciunna
Descendants
[edit]

    • Old Galician-Portuguese:
      • Galician: fonda, funda
      • Portuguese: funda
    • Old Spanish: fonda

  • Gallo-Romance:
    • Catalan: fona, → funda
  • Italo-Romance:
    • Italian: fonda
  • Borrowings:
    • → Koine Greek: φοῦνδα (phoûnda)
      • → Greek: φούντα (foúnta, “tuft”)

Etymology 1

[edit]

Borrowed from Latin funda (“sling”).

Noun

[edit]

funda f (plural fundas)

  1. sling (cloth weapon)
    • Bible, 1 Samuel 17:50
      Portanto, Davi, com uma funda e uma pedra, mostrou ser mais forte que o filisteu, e o entregou à morte, e não havia espada na mão de Davi.
      So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.
    Synonyms: fundíbulo, catapulta
  2. catapult, slingshot (elastic weapon)
    Synonyms: estilingue, atiradeira, bodoque
  3. sling (hanging bandage)
    Synonym: tipoia

Turkish

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From Ottoman Turkish فونده (funda), from Greek φούντα (foúnta, “shrub; flake, fringe”) from Hellenistic φοῦνδα (phoûnda), from Latin funda (“hand-sling, net”).

Noun

[edit]

funda (definite accusative fundayı, plural fundalar)

  1. shrub, heath
  2. (botanics) heath
